text: In 1816, it snowed in June.
Crops died across Europe and North America, and people starved.
The cause was a mountain that exploded more than a year earlier, on the other side of the planet.
April 1815.
On the island of Sumbawa, in what is now Indonesia, Mount Tambora erupted.
It was the largest eruption in recorded history.
The blast was heard on islands more than a thousand miles away.
Ash turned day into night,
and the explosion hurled roughly 150 cubic kilometers of material into the sky.
Thousands died in the blast, the tsunamis and the falling ash.
Famine and disease killed tens of thousands more.
But the most powerful damage was invisible.
Tambora pushed sulfur dioxide high into the stratosphere.
There it turned into tiny sulfate droplets, which spread around the globe.
They formed a veil that reflected sunlight back into space.
The sun was still shining.
But less of its heat was reaching the ground.
Global temperatures dropped by about half a degree Celsius.
That was enough to wreck the seasons.
In New England, snow fell in June.
Frost killed crops in July and August.
In Europe, grain prices soared and bread became unaffordable.
Food riots broke out in cities from France to Switzerland.
In Ireland, typhus spread as starving people wandered the countryside looking for food.
Historians now call it the Year Without a Summer.
Trapped indoors by endless rain, a group of friends gathered at a villa on Lake Geneva.
There was the poet Lord Byron, the poet Percy Shelley, Percy's partner Mary, and their doctor, John Polidori.
To pass the stormy nights, Byron challenged each of them to write a ghost story.
Mary was just eighteen. She couldn't stop thinking about the challenge.
From that gloomy summer came Frankenstein,
a story about a creature brought to life
by a science nobody yet understood.
A volcano on the other side of the world changed the weather, the food and the books we still read today.
Nature's biggest shocks rarely arrive where you expect them.
